content.intro: Learn logging and operational monitoring through a compact visual, an inspectable Django example, and a practical verification task.
content.why_it_matters: Logging and Operational Monitoring matters because a Django project has to behave predictably across requests, database state, configuration, and deployments. Understanding this piece makes the surrounding application easier to test, maintain, and secure.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: This lesson examines logging and operational monitoring as part of deployment and production operations. The objective is to understand the behavior, connect it to the listed subtopics, and verify it with a small example rather than relying on memorized syntax.

content_blocks.title: What to cover
content_blocks.text: The source syllabus for this lesson names: Python logging; Django loggers; Error reporting; Request correlation; Log retention and redaction. Keep these distinct concepts together: know what each item does, when it applies, and what assumption must be verified in your project.

items.title: Python logging
items.text: Logs should include enough structured context to debug events but omit credentials, tokens, payment data and sensitive user content. Define retention, access and alert rules.

items.title: Django loggers
items.text: For Django loggers, identify the Django component responsible, the inputs and outputs it owns, and the boundary conditions that matter. Use the accompanying example as a starting point, verify it with the official versioned documentation, and record one test demonstrating expected behavior.

items.title: Error reporting
items.text: Treat Error reporting as a reproducible diagnostic: capture the exact input and observed result, isolate one hypothesis, and add a regression test once the cause is fixed. Avoid exposing internal stack traces or secrets to public users.

items.title: Request correlation
items.text: Request correlation is part of the request/response contract. Match routes and methods explicitly, return an appropriate response/status, and test success, missing-resource and unauthorized paths.

items.title: Log retention and redaction

Use the accompanying example as a starting point, verify it with the official versioned documentation, and record one test demonstrating expected behavior.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Logging and Operational Monitoring
content_blocks.code:
import logging
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def process_order(order_id):
    logger.info("Processing order", extra={"order_id": order_id})
content_blocks.expected_output: A named logger emits a structured event that can be routed by the LOGGING configuration.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Open a local project using the documented Django 6.1-compatible Python environment. If this snippet depends on model names, URL configuration, settings, or an optional package, add those prerequisites before running it. Otherwise inspect it as a static example. CodeLeaf browser preview does not execute Django/Python server code.
content_blocks.troubleshooting: Never log passwords, raw session values, payment credentials, or private user data. Correlation IDs and retention policy belong in the operational design.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Change one input or configuration choice related to Python logging. Write down the expected outcome, test one normal case and one invalid or boundary case, then record what changed. Do not add real credentials or sensitive production data.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Common pitfalls include skipping a required configuration/import, copying a fragment without its model or URL context, trusting client input, or treating a development-only behavior as production-ready. Check the earliest failing assumption, consult the version-specific docs, and add a regression test for the failure you found.
